questions.enonce_markdown: (a) What was the Sinai Covenant? [4 marks]
questions.corrige_markdown: The Sinai Covenant was the agreement made between God (Yahweh) and the people of Israel at Mount Sinai (Horeb) after their liberation from Egypt (Exodus 19-24). God had brought Israel out of slavery and offered to make them "a kingdom of priests and a holy nation" and his own treasured possession, on condition that they obeyed his voice and kept his covenant (Exodus 19). The people agreed ("All that the Lord has spoken we will do"). God then gave them the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20) and the laws of the Book of the Covenant (Exodus 21-23), and the covenant was ratified with sacrifices and the sprinkling of blood (Exodus 24). It made Israel the people of God, with the law as the guide of their life.
themes: A Level Religious Studies - exodus and moses

questions.enonce_markdown: (b) How central was this covenant for the Israelites? [21 marks]
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The Sinai Covenant was one of several covenants in the Old Testament (with Noah, Abraham, David), but it occupies a very central place in the faith and life of Israel. The biblical writers return to it again and again. Its centrality can be seen in several areas, though it was not the only foundation of Israel's faith.

**1. It created Israel's identity as the people of God.** Before Sinai the Israelites were a group of freed slaves; at Sinai they became "a kingdom of priests and a holy nation" (Exodus 19). The relationship "I will be your God, and you shall be my people" defined who they were and set them apart from other nations.

**2. It provided the moral and legal basis of the nation.** The Ten Commandments (Exodus 20) and the Book of the Covenant (Exodus 21-23) gave Israel her ethical, social and civil laws: duty to God, to parents, to neighbours, protection of the poor, the slave, the stranger, the widow and the orphan. The later law codes in Leviticus and Deuteronomy are understood as an extension of Sinai.

**3. It shaped worship.** Sinai led to the instructions for the tabernacle, the ark, the priesthood and the sacrifices (Exodus 25-31, Leviticus). The festivals of the year (Passover, Weeks, Tabernacles) and the sabbath were interpreted in terms of the covenant. The ark of the covenant, which held the two tablets, was the centre of worship until the time of the monarchy.

**4. It united the tribes.** The twelve tribes were bound together by a common obedience to Yahweh and his law. Later renewal ceremonies (Joshua at Shechem, Joshua 24) reaffirmed this bond, and the tribal league of the period of the judges was held together by the covenant.

**5. It was the standard by which Israel and her kings were judged.** The prophets (Amos, Hosea, Jeremiah and others) accused Israel of covenant breaking: idolatry, injustice and oppression of the poor. The Deuteronomic historians explained the disasters of the nation, including the fall of Samaria and Jerusalem and the exile, as the result of the covenant being broken, while blessings were the reward of obedience (Deuteronomy 28).

**6. It gave a basis for hope and renewal.** Jeremiah looked forward to a "new covenant" written on the heart (Jeremiah 31), a promise that shows how central the idea of covenant remained for Israel's hope.

**Qualification.** The covenant with Abraham (promise of land and descendants) and the covenant with David (a lasting dynasty and Jerusalem) were also fundamental, and some scholars argue that the royal and Zion traditions of Jerusalem gave less weight to Sinai. In practice Israel often failed to keep the covenant: the golden calf (Exodus 32) happened while Moses was still on the mountain. Yet the repeated acts of renewal prove that Israel never abandoned it as the standard.

**Conclusion.** The Sinai Covenant was central: it made Israel a people, gave the law and the pattern of worship, bound the tribes together and became the measure of faithfulness for people, priests, kings and prophets. Even where other covenants were emphasised, Sinai remained the heart of the relationship between Yahweh and Israel.
